metadata.title: Statistical Matching of PISA 2009 and TALIS 2008 Data in Iceland (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD microdata from PISA 2009 and TALIS 2008 for Iceland, but the analysis is conducted at the school level after aggregating student- and teacher-level information to a common unit of analysis. The report describes the original sampling designs (PISA: schools proportional to size then target-age students; TALIS: two-stage stratified probability sample of lower secondary teachers from randomly selected schools), yet it does not report the application of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures in the statistical matching evaluation. Because the core task is statistical matching/imputation of missing components across surveys (rather than estimating achievement model parameters), the manuscript does not specify weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or how they would be used in the matching algorithms. The analytic sample is restricted to matched schools with complete information for matching variables, plus additional exclusions for missingness and influential outliers.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent quantities in this report are not PV-based cognitive achievement scores; instead, the study evaluates statistical matching methods by checking how well synthetic school-level variables reproduce marginal distributions and covariance/correlation structures across PISA and TALIS. The missing-data problem here is unit/item nonresponse induced by the fact that PISA lacks teacher-level data and TALIS lacks student-level data, and the methods compared are hot-deck matching and multiple-imputation-style statistical matching procedures. Missing-data handling is therefore addressed through multiple imputation and related imputation mechanisms rather than PV generation/combining.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study focuses on Iceland and uses only schools for which both PISA 2009 and TALIS 2008 data can be matched. Of 142 participating schools, 122 were matchable; 20 unmatched schools were excluded, and an additional 39 schools were excluded due to large amounts of missing data on variables required for the matching procedures. Five further schools were excluded as influential outliers, leaving 78 schools with full information from both surveys. For the experimental proof-of-concept, the authors duplicated the Iceland data and then removed PISA data for half the sample and TALIS data for the other half, yielding 78 schools with PISA data and 78 schools with TALIS data (missingness treated as missing completely at random due to the random deletion).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report evaluates statistical matching methods to create a synthetic cohort that combines PISA 2009 (student and school principal data) with TALIS 2008 (teacher and school principal data) for Iceland, where the surveys do not share the same units. Because the only common unit across surveys is the school, the study aggregates student- and teacher-level information to the school level and then matches schools using shared principal-reported variables. Six matching/imputation approaches are compared, including hot-deck distance matching (nearest-neighbor Euclidean distance) and multiple-imputation-based methods (stochastic regression imputation, predictive mean matching, Bayesian regression imputation via chained equations, Bayesian bootstrap predictive mean matching, and an EM bootstrap). Validity is assessed using Rässler (2002) criteria focused on preserving covariance/correlation structure (third level) and marginal distributions (fourth level). Results indicate that most methods reproduce marginal descriptive statistics reasonably well, while BBPMM and the EM bootstrap stand out as best at preserving the conditional covariance/correlation structure and producing the closest distributional shapes (e.g., Q-Q plots). The report frames this as a proof of concept for feasibility, while noting limitations such as aggregation to the school level and the need for further work on sampling variability and sensitivity to imputation error.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a methodological/data-linking evaluation rather than an empirical ML prediction study: it compares statistical matching and imputation algorithms to preserve validity criteria, without training supervised ML models on a predictive target variable. Consequently, there is no ML algorithm “best model” for a prediction metric, and the main_findings table is intentionally left empty to avoid fabricating StructuredFinding rows. The report’s outcomes are validity checks (marginal distributions and conditional covariance/correlation structure) rather than predictive performance (e.g., accuracy/AUC/R²) for a defined target variable.
